paragraphs.heading: A rock rich in aluminium
paragraphs.text: Bauxite is a sedimentary rock that holds a relatively large share of aluminium. Worldwide, it is the main source of both aluminium and gallium. The rock looks dull and can be reddish-brown, white or tan. Its name goes back to 1821, when the French geologist Pierre Berthier discovered it near Les Baux, a village in Provence in southern France.

paragraphs.heading: What it is made of
paragraphs.text: Most of bauxite is a mix of three aluminium minerals called gibbsite, boehmite and diaspore. Mixed in with them are two iron oxides, goethite and hematite, along with kaolinite, which is an aluminium clay mineral. There are also small amounts of two more minerals, anatase and ilmenite. Which form the aluminium takes decides the conditions needed to extract it.

paragraphs.heading: How it forms
paragraphs.text: Lateritic bauxites are found mostly in tropical countries. They formed from silicate rocks such as granite, basalt and shale through a process called lateritization. Making bauxite this way depends on intense weathering in a place with very good drainage, which lets kaolinite dissolve and gibbsite come out of solution. Another kind, carbonate bauxite, sits above limestone and dolomite, mainly in Europe, Guyana, Suriname and Jamaica. There, clay that was scattered through the limestone became concentrated as the limestone around it slowly dissolved during chemical weathering.

paragraphs.heading: Mining near the surface
paragraphs.text: Most of the world's bauxite deposits lie within 1 to 20 metres of the Earth's surface. Bauxite is almost always close to the top of the ground with little or nothing covering it, so it is usually strip mined. Guinea produces the most, followed by Australia and China.

paragraphs.heading: From rock to aluminium oxide
paragraphs.text: The ore is usually heated with a sodium hydroxide solution in a pressure vessel, at 150 to 200 °C. At these temperatures the aluminium dissolves as sodium aluminate. This is the Bayer process. The leftover residue is filtered off. Cooling the liquid and then seeding it with fine grains of aluminium hydroxide makes pure gibbsite settle out. The gibbsite is usually heated to more than 1,000 °C, which turns it into aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃.

paragraphs.heading: From oxide to metal
paragraphs.text: The aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite at about 960 °C. An electric current passed through this molten material can then yield metallic aluminium. This electrolysis step is called the Hall–Héroult process, after its American and French discoverers.

paragraphs.heading: Once dearer than gold
paragraphs.text: Before the Hall–Héroult process was invented, and before another one called the Deville process, aluminium ore was refined by heating it in a vacuum with elemental sodium or potassium. The method was complicated, and it used up materials that were themselves expensive at the time. As a result, early aluminium metal cost more than gold. Recycling aluminium needs less electric power than making it from ore, and more recycling may considerably extend the world's bauxite reserves.

paragraphs.heading: A risky cargo
paragraphs.text: Shipped in bulk, bauxite may liquefy if it is too moist. Liquefaction, together with what is called the free surface effect, can make the cargo shift rapidly inside the hold. That can leave the ship unstable and may sink it. One vessel suspected of having been lost this way is the MS Bulk Jupiter, in 2015.
